title: The First Bill Is Paid in Full

blocks.text: The kit room of the Ninefold Hall, at dawn. Gideon Pask was humming a tune nobody in the Bole knows.
"From when I was a boy, chick," he said, and set a bottle of pinned ink in my palm. One per surveyor per quarter.
Brisk signed for hers and told him she was twenty-nine.
I uncapped mine and wrote line one of my first Form 9, because the form says to start with the obvious.
My given name is Linnet.
Footnote: it was the last morning that line was true.

Survey Form 9 is one page. It has eleven ruled lines, a signature box, and a warning printed along the foot in letters small enough to ignore: Writing a fact in pinned ink does not protect the fact. Every trainee ignores it once. I ignored it for eleven lines.
I did not fill all eleven. I wrote five more.
I can read Survey shorthand at ninety words a minute.
I remember my mother teaching me a bowline on the kitchen table.
I mark my footnotes with a dagger, and have since I was seven.
I want the Chainman's licence.
I cannot swim.
Footnote: I would not hate to lose the last one. I put it down so the form would know I am honest.
Gideon leaned over the counter to read it upside down, which is against Standing Order 3.4 and which he has done to every trainee for forty years. He stopped humming.
"Want isn't a fact, chick."
"It's a fact about me, sir. A stranger could check it. Ask anyone in the cohort."
"Ha." He tapped the bottle in my hand. "Three bottles of pinned ink and a prayer, that's the stores this quarter. Don't blot."
I did not blot.
Cressida Vesey came in at six exactly. She is sixty, grey, and has never in my hearing been early or late. She put a pin card on the counter in front of me, face up, and kept two fingers on it.
"Ardent. Provisional card. Weirside. Finish it."
I read it twice. A pin card has six fields. This one had five filled.

Branch: Weirside. Distance: 1. Doors: Ninefold, east wall, third from the left; Weirside hall, the same. Route: read by the Exchange Desk daily for twenty-one years. Hinge: Tessary weir, the weir night.
Hinge-maker: blank.
"The Desk has read this route every day for twenty-one years," I said. "And nobody filled in whose decision it was?"
"Is that on the card?"
"No."
"Then that is the job." She lifted her fingers. "Three of us. Brisk opens. You accompany."
"Standing Order 4.2," I said. "Trainees accompany a crew and may not open doors."
"And?"
"And Survey custom. The first bill is paid in full." I said it the way it is written in the Trainee Handbook, page one, in a box. "No ballast on a first crossing. Whatever the branch takes, I pay."
"Good." She was already turning away.
I looked at the hinge field again. Tessary weir, the weir night. Under it, in the Desk's small hand, the date. Twenty-two years ago, at the spring high water.
I know that date. Everybody in my house knows that date. It is the night my father went out to the weir in the rain to help with the sluice gates and did not come home.
Brisk was watching me over her ink bottle. Gideon had started humming again, then stopped.
"Noted," I said.

Footnote: Survey custom assigns trainees to near branches by rota. I checked the rota afterwards. My name was on it in the right place, in the right ink. I filed that under coincidence, where it stayed for some time.

The threshold room of the Ninefold Hall has nine doors. They are oak, iron-strapped, and older than anything else in Tessary that still has a roof. Each one stands in its own stone frame in a bare wall and opens onto nothing on our side. You can walk round behind them. Every trainee does, on the first day, and feels foolish.
The Exchange Desk sits in the middle of the floor. The day clerk had a packet of Weirside letters tied with tape and looked at us the way a man looks at a crew that is about to spend his opening.
"All yours," he said. "Letters wait till tomorrow, then."

Footnote: each pair of branches opens once per day from each side. If Brisk read the Bole's side for us, nobody in the Bole could open to Weirside again until dawn. The clerk had a point. He also had a newspaper.
Cressida and Brisk had made their ballast at home that morning. I didn't see it. That is the whole point of ballast. A witness spoils it.
Brisk stood in the third doorway with her toes on the line of the sill, rolled her shoulders, and patted the stone like a horse's neck.
"Morning, old girl," she said to the door. Then, in a different voice, flat and clear, she read the route. "Tessary weir. The weir night."

The door did not swing. It does not swing. The dark space inside the frame went pale, then bright, and then there was a room in it, the same room, seen from where the wall should have been, with a different clerk at a different desk.
"Door's open," Brisk said. "Nine. Eight. Move, people."
Cressida stepped through. I stepped through after her. Entering costs nothing. You pay on the way out.
"Seven," Brisk said, from behind me, and came through on six, and the door went dark on her heels as if she had shut it with her shoulder.
Weirside's Ninefold Hall is ours with different curtains. Green, not brown. The nine doors are the same nine doors. They have to be. If anyone ever changes a frame, the door dies for that pair.
"Bole crew," said the Weirside clerk, a young man with ink on his chin. "We held our opening for you. You'll want it tonight." He pointed his pen at the desk. "And she left that for the trainee."
There was an envelope on the blotter, addressed: For Trainee Ardent, Bole Survey. The handwriting was mine. Slightly rounder. Mine, if I had been a little less tired for twenty years.
I opened it. Two lines.
When you leave, it will take your name. It is the oldest thing you have that I don't.
He's well. Don't come to see him; it costs more than a name.
No signature. She didn't need one.
I read it twice and put it in my Form 9 folder, behind the bill, which is against Standing Order 3.7, which covers what may be kept with a bill. I didn't care.

When I looked up, a woman was crossing the far end of the hall, past the ninth door. Survey coat. Satchel. My height. My walk, which I have only ever seen in shop windows. My face, turned a little away. She did not look at us. She did not slow down. She went out through the arch into the stair, and her footsteps went down, quick, the way I take stairs when I am late.
Brisk said, "Was that..."
"Is it on the card?" said Cressida.
"No, chief."
"Then we have a registry to find."
Footnote: she knew I was coming. She knew what the swap would take. She knew which name to warn me about. I had four questions and no one to put them to, so I made a list.
1. How did she know the rota?
2. Why write and not wait?
3. Who is "he"?
4. I knew who he was.
Footnote to the footnote: number four is not a question. I was not at my best.

Weirside's Tessary is our Tessary for most of a mile. The river runs the same way. The bridge is the same bridge. The bakers on Quay Street are the same bakers, and they gave Brisk the same look ours give her.
The weir is not the same.

In the Bole, the Tessary weir has a stone memorial on the east bank, a plain slab with the names of the four men who drowned on the weir night. I have read it more times than I can count. My father's name is third.
In Weirside there is no slab. There is a bench. Two old men were sitting on it, eating bread, watching the water go over the sill.
I stopped walking. Cressida stopped one pace later. She didn't ask me why. She looked at the bench, and at the place on the bank where the slab would have been, and then at her watch.
"Registry closes at four," she said.

The Weirside registry is in the old customs court behind the Fishmarket. Same building. Same clerk's counter, worn into a dip in the same place. Cressida showed her Cartographer's warrant, and the registrar, who had seen Bole crews before, brought us the books without being asked twice.

Archive work is what surveyors actually do. It is not glamorous. It is a pencil, a ruler and a great deal of dust. You find a hinge by finding the place where two records disagree, and then you find the person whose decision made them disagree.

Death register, spring, twenty-two years ago. I ran the ruler down the week of the high water. Two deaths in Weir Ward that month. One old woman, of age. One infant, of fever. No drownings. Not at the weir. Not anywhere.
"Four men drowned at the Bole weir that night," I said. "Here, none."
"And the other three?" said Cressida.
I checked the ward roll for each name from the slab. All three alive in Weirside, at least that year. I wrote them in my notebook.
Then I turned the ward roll to Weir Ward, this year's, and found the A's.
Ardent, Hesper. Sluice Row, number eleven.
Ardent, Tobin. Sluice Row, number eleven. Occupation: sluice hand, Tessary weir.
I put the ruler down very carefully, parallel to the spine of the book.
Footnote: my father's name was Tobin Ardent. I have not written it often. There has never been a form that needed it.
Brisk was reading over my shoulder, which I allowed. She said nothing at all, which from Brisk is a speech.
"Weir-watch log," said Cressida to the registrar. "The night in question."

It was a thin book with a split spine. The sergeant of the watch had kept it in pencil, in a hand like barbed wire. The night of the high water: men called to the sluices at nine. Names ticked as they arrived. Four names ticked. One name with a line through it and a note in the margin.
Ardent, T. Stood down. Wife asked him to stay home.

That was the hinge. Not the water. The water came in both branches. In the Bole, my mother watched him put on his coat and did not ask him to stay. In Weirside, she asked, and he stayed. And the three other men, who in the Bole went down with him? I checked. The watch went short-handed. They opened the gates two hours later. The sill held. Nobody drowned.
One woman, one sentence, one night. Heavy enough that the world could not hold both.
I made a list. I always make a list.
1. My father is alive in this branch.
2. He lives eleven minutes' walk from this counter. I timed the route from the map on the wall.
3. In this branch he has a daughter who is me, and who asked me not to come.
4. The registry closes at four. It is a quarter to three.
5. Hinge-maker: Hesper Ardent. My mother.
There was one more book on the counter. Birth register. I opened it to the year without being asked, because the ruler was still in my hand and I wanted to know.
Ardent, Sabeth. Weir Ward. Same day as mine. Same hour. Father: Tobin Ardent. Mother: Hesper Ardent.
Not Linnet. In Weirside I was never Linnet.
I stood up.
"I'd like to go to Sluice Row," I said. "For the card. To confirm the address. It is good practice to confirm an address."
Cressida did not look up from the watch log.
"And your bill says?"

I opened the folder. My bill was on top. Six lines in my own hand. Things I would hate to lose. My name. My shorthand. My mother at the kitchen table with a length of cord. My dagger. My licence that I didn't have yet. Not swimming.
There was nothing on it about him. There couldn't be. A fact about another person isn't a fact about you. And behind the bill, the note: Don't come to see him; it costs more than a name.

She was not talking about swaps. A visit costs no swap. Facts you make inside a branch are agreed by it and never taken there. You can walk down Sluice Row and knock and walk away again for free, according to every clause in the Handbook.
The cost was on the other side of the door. A man opening it to his daughter, and his daughter not being her. And her, somewhere on the stair, having to explain me.
"My bill says I'm here to finish a card," I said.
"Then finish it."
I sat down. I took out the pin card. I uncapped the pinned ink, because pin cards are kept in it, and in the sixth field I wrote: Hesper Ardent. The ink went on black and stayed black.
At the foot is the surveyor's signature box. Survey custom is surnames. I signed it Ardent, Tr.
Footnote: so the card never needed to know my first name either.

We had an hour before the registry closed and four before the opening, and Cressida does not waste an hour. She had me check every field of the card against the books again, aloud. She sat across the table and followed each line with one finger, saying nothing.
On the fourth line I asked her a procedural question.
"Is there a clause for the family?"
"Which family?"
"The hinge-maker's. When we name one. Do we tell them? That they did this?" I gestured at the window, at Weirside, at the bench where the slab should be.
"There is no notification clause."
"Should there be?"
"Is there evidence it would help anyone?"
"I don't know. If it were your mother. If someone came and told you that your mother's one decision on one night had split..."
I stopped, because she had stopped. Not her finger on the line. Her face. It was very still, the way a face goes when it reaches for a word and the word is not on the shelf.
"My mother," Cressida said.
She waited for something. I waited with her. A cart went past outside. The registrar shut a drawer.
"Field four," Cressida said. "You've transposed the folio numbers. Thirty-one, not thirteen."
I had. I corrected it.

Footnote: she knows the clause numbers of the whole Handbook and the folio of every card she has ever checked. She could not tell me one thing about her mother. Not even a sentence that started and ended. I didn't ask again. I would like that on the record as tact rather than cowardice. It may have been both.

At dusk we went back to Weirside's hall. The clerk with ink on his chin had gone home. A night clerk was at the desk, eating soup, and had kept the opening as promised. Nothing had gone through the door all day from his side.

Cressida and Brisk checked the seals on their kit, which means checking their ballast without looking at it, which is a skill I did not yet have. I had nothing to check. The first bill is paid in full.
The woman with my face did not come back. I looked at the arch to the stair four times. Brisk saw me do it and said nothing, which from Brisk is now two speeches.
Brisk stood in the third doorway from the left, Weirside hall's door to the Ninefold, and patted the frame.
"Evening, old girl. Same again." And then, flat and clear: "Tessary weir. The weir night."
The dark inside the frame went pale, then bright, and there was our threshold room, brown curtains, our day clerk gone, our night clerk looking up.
"Door's open. Nine. Eight. Move, people."
Cressida went through on eight. Brisk said, "Ardent," on seven, which means go, and I went on seven, and she came through on five.
You pay on the way out. The Handbook says you feel it at the doorway. It is not wrong.
It is not pain. It is the feeling of coming downstairs in the dark and finding one step fewer than your foot expected. You stand on the landing and you know a step is gone, and you cannot tell which.

"Clean," said Brisk behind me, patting her pocket. Her ballast had gone. Cressida touched her own cuff and nodded once. Hers had gone too. One ballast each, one kind spent in Weirside, nothing that mattered to anyone. Their counterparts would wake up holding something small and pointless that they had never made, and lose nothing.
Mine had nothing to take but something that mattered.

Footnote, added later at my desk, with the bill open: here is the order the swap runs, which is called Least Agreement, which I could recite at the age of fifteen and had never before had to do on myself.
One. A hinge fact. If I had ever made a decision heavy enough to split the world, Weirside would have reached for it first. I had not. I was a trainee who wanted a licence. Nothing to take.

Two. Glare. Something I carried that Weirside could not hold, because something it depends on doesn't exist there. Weirside is one hinge from home. It has everything we have, except a stone slab. Nothing to take.
Three. Ballast. None. First bill, paid in full.
Four. Orphans. Facts that nothing in Weirside supports. Oldest goes first. The oldest thing I had that nothing in Weirside agreed with was my given name. Weirside's register says Sabeth.
So it took Linnet, and gave me Sabeth.

Footnote to that footnote: she pays too. The counterpart always pays. Somewhere on Sluice Row, or on a stair, or at a desk, a woman with my face felt a step go out from under her at the same moment I did. She gave up the name she was born with. She knew it was coming. She wrote me a note about it, and she did not ask me for anything, and she did not stop to be thanked.

Back in the Bole, our night clerk was writing in the door log. "Back, then," he said. "Three out, three in. Vesey, Brisk..." He looked at me, and his pen hovered for half a second, and then he wrote. "Ardent."
"Ardent," Cressida agreed. She took the Weirside card from my folder and set it on his desk. "Filed."
"Good work, Ardent," said Brisk, and thumped my shoulder.
Gideon was still in the kit room when we passed, though it was past eight. He looked up from a ledger and said, "All home, chick? All whole?"
"Clean, sir," said Brisk.
"Ardent?"
"Paid in full," I said.
"That's the girl. That's the way." He went back to humming.

Footnote: nobody used my first name between the threshold room and the street. Nobody ever does. Survey custom is surnames. It is a good custom. I recommend it to anyone. It means you can lose your name in a doorway and walk the whole length of the Ninefold Hall to the front steps, past four people who know you, and no one in the building notices, least of all you.
At the steps, Cressida stopped me with two fingers on my sleeve.
"Your bill," she said. "Read it at home. Sitting down."
"Protocol is to read it at the threshold, chief."
"Is it?"

It is. Standing Order 9.1. She knows it is. She looked at me with no expression at all, and then she went down the steps and turned left toward the river without saying goodnight. She never says goodnight.
Footnote: kind in actions, never in words. I didn't understand that yet. I thought she had forgotten the clause.

Our house is on Weir Lane, which runs down to the river a quarter-mile below the slab. The lamp was lit in the kitchen. My mother was at the table with the account book open, the way she is every evening, her reading glasses pushed up into her hair.

I stood in the kitchen doorway and looked at her. Hesper Ardent. Hinge-maker. Her name in black on a pin card in the Ninefold Hall, in my handwriting, for as long as there is a Survey. I had not decided whether I would tell her. I had not decided anything. I had just stood in a registry and read about the night she let him go.
She looked up and smiled.
"Sabeth. There you are. Your supper's in the oven, it'll be dry as a boot."
"Thank you," I said.
It sounded right. That was the worst of it. It sounded like my name. It is my name. The records say so, and she has said it ten thousand times, and every one of those times has quietly agreed.
I ate the supper. It was dry as a boot. I told her the job had gone well, which was true. I told her nothing else, which was a choice.
Then I went up to my room and sat on the bed, because I had been told to sit down, and I opened the Form 9 folder and took out my bill.
Six lines in pinned ink, in my own hand. Five of them read true.
Shorthand. Bowline. Dagger. Licence. Swimming.
The first line read:
My given name is Linnet.
I read it four times. It was my handwriting and my ink, and I had written it that morning, and I knew exactly what it told me. It told me what had gone.
It did not tell me why anyone would want it back.
Linnet. I said it aloud, once, to the dark, and it meant nothing to me at all.
